explanation: Guido of Arezzo took ut, re, mi, fa, sol and la from a Latin hymn whose lines each start a step higher. Italians later switched to 'do', which is easier to sing.

claims.text: In solmization, do replaced the older syllable ut.
Si and ti are names for the seventh note of the scale, and sa begins the Indian sargam; do replaced none of them.
Guido of Arezzo took the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol and la from a Latin hymn, Ut queant laxis.
Each line of Ut queant laxis begins a step higher than the line before.
Italian musicians replaced ut with do because do is easier to sing.

writerNotes: Self-check (§9.3). Lint: clean under content:check for writer w-pmusic01w. Claims: every checkable statement in the stem, options and explanation is listed, with risk at or above the C26 floor and raised where a fact is beyond everyday knowledge. Datasets: no pinned dataset covers these music facts (the manifest holds geographic, scientific, Nobel, Olympic and art-collection data), so each high-risk claim needs web evidence from the checkers. I used no WebSearch. Rival test: argued for si, the old name of the seventh syllable (later ti), and sa, the opening syllable of Indian sargam; neither is the syllable do replaced. A reasoner can strike si and ti as names of the seventh note, which leaves the foothold. French musicians still use ut in formal key names. Volatility: evergreen; no time words, and nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026. Regional: solfège is taught worldwide, and the Indian sa gives South Asian players a plausible trap rather than an advantage. Style: Oxford spelling, straight quotes, no en or em dashes, explanation within 35 words. Myths: screened against myths.json, no hit. Mystery: not applicable to a practice item. Encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: c5 gives the usual reason (an open vowel); the change is often credited to Giovanni Battista Doni, whom I left out.
